1#main: The law of a doubtful firstborn, caesarean birth, tumtum, and androgynous. In it are 7 seifim. A doubtful firstborn—the owners need not give it to the kohen; rather they delay it until a blemish befalls it and they eat it; and it is forbidden in shearing and work. And if a kohen seized it, they do not remove it from his hand. {Rama: And some say they remove it from the kohen immediately (Tur in the name of the Rosh). And so is the halachah. And even if the Israelite gave it to him mistakenly thinking he must give it, and afterward it became known to him—the kohen must return it to him (Piskei Maharai siman 166).}
2#main: A caesarean birth and one born after him through the womb—both are not firstborn; even if she bore a female first by caesarean and a male afterward through the womb, since another preceded. A firstborn that is a tumtum—behold it is a doubtful firstborn and it is eaten in its blemished state by the owners. And specifically when it urinates from the place of females; but if it urinates from the place of males, it is certainly a firstborn and must be given to the kohen. (Tur in the name of the Rosh, and not like the Rambam.)
3#main: An androgynous animal is a doubtful firstborn and is eaten in its blemished state by the owners.
4#main: An animal that gave birth when full and returned empty—the one born after it is a doubtful firstborn, lest she miscarried something that does not release from the firstborn obligation.
5#main: A ewe that bore in the form of a goat, or a goat that bore in the form of a ewe—is exempt from the firstborn, as it says, "but the firstborn of an ox"—until it is an ox and its firstborn is an ox. And if it had some signs of its mother, behold it is a firstborn, and it has a permanent blemish—for you have no greater blemish than a change in its creation. (Rambam's wording, chapter 5 of Laws of Firstborn, halachah 6.)
6#main: A cow that bore in the form of a donkey—and it has some signs of a cow—behold it is a firstborn for the kohen, since the donkey species has firstborn law. But if it bore in the form of a horse or camel—even though it has some signs of a cow—behold it is a doubtful firstborn; therefore it is eaten by the owners, and if a kohen seized it they do not remove it from his hand. And the same applies to a donkey that bore in the form of a horse and has some signs of a donkey—this is a doubtful firstborn. (And it was already explained that if a kohen seized it, they remove it from his hand.)
7#main: A small animal that miscarried a dissolved fetus—meaning the embryo melted and the discharge emerged—it is exempt from the firstborn, and one must show it to a wise shepherd to see if it is fetal discharge. And a large animal that miscarried a placenta is exempt from the firstborn; and the placenta itself has no sanctity and may be fed to dogs. An animal that discharged a blood clot is exempt from the firstborn, and the clot is buried to publicize that it is exempt from the firstborn.
